"The Doll" (1938) is a Polish film, directed by Michał Waszyński, and based on the novel "Lalka" by Bolesław Prus. The original Polish title of the film is "Lalka." The story set in the 19th century in Poland, revolves around a young and ambitious merchant named Stanisław Wokulski. He struggles with his unrequited love for a woman named Izabela Łęcka, who belongs to a deteriorating high-class society.

The film explores themes of love, social disparity, and the pursuit of status, reflecting the complexities of human relationships within the context of societal expectations and class differences. Stanisław Wokulski, despite his rising status as a self-made man, faces challenges in bridging the societal gap that separates him from his beloved Izabela.

"The Doll" is notable for its costume design, period detail, and its portrayal of the Polish society during the partition period when Poland was divided between Russia, Prussia, and Austria. Michał Waszyński, the director, was recognized for his ability to capture the essence of the novel, although, as it often happens with literary adaptations, some elements of the book might have been condensed or altered for cinematic purposes.

The film is considered an important work in Polish cinema, particularly for its adaptation of one of Poland’s significant literary works. While not as well-known internationally as some other classic European films, "The Doll" has an esteemed place in Polish cultural history.
